newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Rafsanjani says U.S., Israel pressure Bonn.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Rafsanjani says U.S., Israel pressure Bonn.

text.p: Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani said on Friday the German government was under U.S. and Israeli pressure but said he hoped Bonn would prevent tensions in ties with Tehran from spiralling out of control.

Rafsanjani said Iran hoped to continue its friendship with its biggest trade partner despite strains over the trial of five men for the 1992 killing of three Kurdish dissidents and their translator in Berlin. Prosecutors last week accused Tehran of ordering the murders.
"Satan's agents work so hard to change cooperation into conflict," he said in a prayer sermon at Tehran University.
"We still believe that the German government's policy has nothing to do with the court's action. We should not forget that the German government is under the pressure of the U.S. and Israeli agents."
The crowd chanted "Death to America" and "Death to Israel" during the sermon which was broadcast live on Tehran radio.
But Rafsanjani said the Iranian and German governments should work together.
"I hope we will be able to continue our friendship and cooperation with the German government," he said.

"We hope that the German government is careful so that this (situation) does not lead to a point that neither we nor they want...when the leaders of the two countries cannot control it anymore," he said.
His remarks came one day after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl told Rafsanjani he was concerned about a deterioration in relations between the two countries.
In a two-page letter Kohl told Rafsanjani German courts were independent and that the government had absolutely no control over or involvement in the so-called "Mykonos trial".
Kohl assured Rafsanjani that the trial in Berlin was not "a political trial", but a criminal trial.

The German prosecutors' accusations against Iranian leaders have provoked outrage in Iran. Protesters have rallied outside the German embassy in Tehran, pelting the compound with eggs and tomatoes and calling for the death of the prosecutors.
In Germany, a member of Kohl's cabinet has echoed the accusations against Iranian leaders and called for an end to Bonn's policy of "critical dialogue" with Tehran.

"Iran's state terrorism against those who think differently has once again become visible as a result of this trial," Development Minister Carl-Dieter Spranger said in Thursday's edition of the Bild daily.
The prosecutors have demanded life sentences for two of the defendants in the Berlin trial -- an Iranian and a Lebanese.
Rafsanjani said: "The German court, under the covert or overt influence of the U.S. and Israeli agents, perhaps knowingly or otherwise, is harming these good ties."
"Of course, I shall send a reply to Mr Kohl and you will be made aware of my reply," he said.
"We have no doubt that the people of Germany wish to be sincere and cooperate with our great nation. We have enjoyed good ties throughout history," Rafsanjani said.
